items.title: BOOK on BOOKS: 21 Futures, Tales From the Timechain
items.text:
In my ever-hungry attempts at Denstravaganzas, I must pile onto the B\&A territory (all my econ attempts are failing/falling short of the extremely competitive marketplace over there!)

Alas, more BOOK on BOOKs... because I've been neglecting that. https://stacker.news/items/1613346?commentId=1613391

My impression is that this bitcoin-themed future/fiction play from a few years ago died down quite a bit?

[*21 Futures: Tales from the Timechain*](https://link.amazon/B025NHagp) was a cute collection of futuristic bitcoin stories from, *almost to the date* three years ago. Our dollar exchange rate is 88% up from that moment; CPI about 10% higher; gold at smack-on 100%; NVIDIA stock... (https://stacker.news/items/877723) lol, even *after* today's debacle, 235% higher. Guess that tells you what you *should* have been doing during the last three years.

(Also, I believe I have a code at [Konsensus ](https://konsensus.net/books/?b=21-futures-tales-from)--  BOOK  -- in case you were ordering stuffz): 

![](https://m.stacker.news/165785)

## "Remember the words, Vincent. Just remember the damn words!"

***

> In its first stand-alone publication, the Bitcoiner powerhouse Konsensus Network brings something quite unique to Bitcoinland: fiction. Mostly known as a collaboration for publishing Bitcoin books translated into various European languages, since Knut Svanholm’s flagship[ *Everything Divided by 21 Million*](https://link.amazon/B0dSDe1bG) \[no more; Knut's books are in his own shop, Bitcoin Infinity store] a few years ago, **Konsensus is now becoming a publishing house in its own right.** 

> In *21 Futures*, the first Bitcoin fiction anthology, we are treated to 21 short stories by 21 excellent authors, most of whom are unknown to you. All tales imagine a far-off future where bitcoin has already won, their authors trying to divine what a hyperbitcoinized world or universe actually looks like. I say “universe” because in true Extropian spirit, about half of the stories are space-related and hyper-futuristic, filled with robots, cryonics, or mining endeavors in faraway star systems. Flint and Iris, for instance, are **two kids in a struggling family on a refueling hub a million miles from Earth who see their lives radically change when they find a discarded OPENDIME with 0.25 BTC on it.** Johanna buys half a mining planet with locally mined bitcoin during a meteor shower blackout where the colony lost its connection to Earth’s mainchain.

## "Two tales have wild goose chases after inherited bitcoin, where the journey itself might be more valuable than the reward; one is personal and took months, while the other is political and took decades."

> The myriad of authors use humor, pain, colorful descriptions, vivid characters, and fast-paced action. Some tales are captivating; others funny, cringe-worthy, or on occasion rather dull. There are self-contained stories that leave the reader content and smiling, while others seem unfinished with plot lines left unexplored.

> Some imagine the supernatural nature of Satoshi. Some are mystical and futuristic. All are weird; playfully weird; Bitcoiner weird. We are treated to millisats and Finneys, the latter being “a subdivide of sats named after Hal Finney” (page 44). Clara, imbibing a truth-serum — a not-so-subtle metaphor for orange-pilling — sees “the source code of the universe, equations as living tendrils of light materializing into particles, planets, and stars” (page 129). In one illuminating dialogue that follows, Clara’s apologist opponent nonchalantly states, “It’s how things are”, to which Clara powerfully responds “It’s how things *were*” (page 132).

> **One segment, where a mob attacked a bank branch, seems more fact than fiction in 2023: “WE WANT OUR MONEY”, they shout;** “These people weren’t there to rob or loot the bank. They only wanted what was rightfully theirs — or it should have been before the government decreed otherwise and stole billions in one go” (page 142).

> In the most terrifying yet uplifting of the many visions *21 Futures* presents, the aliens are already here and they are actively acquiring our bitcoin: “At this juncture”, reads the memo sent out by the Emerging Civilizations Council in the story, “the galactic playbook permits members to approach a pre-federation civilization undetected in order to fairly attain small quantities of their local implementation of inviolable absolute scarcity” (page 242).

> The book is impeccably edited and tastefully assembled, and the AI-inspired art does a lot to aesthetically complement the stories. “Only stories have the power to stop us, to wake us, to make us feel rather than think”, (page vii) lead editor Philip Charter powerfully observes in the opening remarks.

> True. Dat.

**SELECTED QUOTES:**

* “It isn’t just the vast chasm between noderoids and clear-bloods that disturbs me. It is the undeniable rift growing between us noderoids — each lost in our cycles, each becoming more machine than the last” (page 36).
* “Slowly, yet with unyielding certainty, the kingdom shifted over the years. It changed not through a coup or uprising but through a still, relentless force, like water eroding stone. As the seasons passed and more villagers imbibed the Elysian brew, the weight of their invisible chains lessened, their atoms scattering into the evening air” (page 133).
* “Vincent stood at this threshold, poised between the familiar and the abhorrent. Shadows danced around him, their macabre waltz an unsettling omen of the horrors that awaited within the village. Yet, driven by determination, Vincent summoned the courage to push on, to brave the unknown that dwelled within the unhallowed embrace of this accursed place. ‘*Remember the words, Vincent. Just remember the damn words*.’”(page 54).
* “No need to worry, my English crumpet! Our back-of-the-napkin calculations suggest that, with a little help from the Texas of the North, there’s enough flared natural gas in the U.S. to run the entire bitcoin network” (page 168).

you remember this @realBitcoinDog?! *you and that* *little English crumpet!*

***

*Just as with the* Gradually, Then Suddenly *review (*https://stacker.news/items/1536970*), I believe this review was featured in* [*The Halving Issue (Q1, 2024)*](https://bitcoinmagazine.com/print/the-halving-issue-letter-from-the-editors)*, but can't be sure... same BM issue anyway; online backlog and ToC of past magazines are removed from the website and I don't have all my physical mags with me.*

***

## BOOK on BOOKS Archive

*Going Infinite*, by Michael Lewis (https://stacker.news/items/1604939

items.title: How Much Should Anthropic Pop? (Money Stuff, Matt Levine)
items.text:
Here's a forgotten one from the other week... and it's AI days and IPO next week(ish?) and with a funky, exciting [Predyx market attached](https://beta.predyx.com/market/anthropic-ipo-closing-market-cap-1781739293?ref=PREDYXTZ0UUNOP).

STANDARD game theory/media-marketing strategy is to *slightly* underprice your IPO so that there's a pop on day 1, everyone who subscribed feel good about themselves, and the investment bankers don't get a bunch of shit for finding the *wrong* price.

## So... how much should $ANT pop?!

**20% *obviously***. It is known.

> a really important thing we have learned about finance in the last few years is that prediction markets are pretty accurate. That is: If you have a platform where people can make real-money bets on some outcome, their bets will tend to give a pretty accurate and well-calibrated estimate of the actual outcome. **Kalshi event contracts are not tied to, like, election outcomes or football scores by arbitrage mechanisms, and in the abstract Kalshi could just be wrong about everything.**

so by implication, *you can already trade non-IPOd companies on offshore, unregulated prediction markets!*

With the track records of SpaceX and Cerebras, Hyperliquid has been pretty good. Thought experiment with OpenAI:

> The price of OpenAI on Hyperliquid on the afternoon of the IPO<sup>\[2]</sup> will predict the opening price of OpenAI on the stock exchange the day after the IPO about as well as the closing price of Tesla stock on Nasdaq today will predict the opening price of Tesla on Nasdaq tomorrow: not perfectly (news happens, etc.), but in a reasonably continuous way. And let’s say that everyone knows this: The pre-IPO perpetual futures get lots of news coverage, they are routinely referenced by analysts and investors and bankers, they are part of everyone’s understanding of the IPO process

![](https://m.stacker.news/166125)

Can we just get *rid of the investment bankers and pre-IPO shopping around?!*

* **Strategy 1:** You price the IPO efficiently at $120 because that *is* the best guess of fair market value
* **Strategy 2:** You price the IPO non-efficiently at $100 because that way, everybody will get a neat 20% pop, and we're all happy. *Repeat game* idea.

> All of the investors in the IPO will have an immediate mark-to-market profit, though most of them will not cash out: You have placed the IPO shares mostly with long-term fundamental investors who believe in the company’s vision, not with fast-money flippers, and you want to reward their belief with a quick profit.

Strategy 2 *does* come at the uncomfortable cost:

> If it deliberately prices it cheap, it is transferring billions of dollars of value from the company (and its pre-IPO shareholders) to its banks’ hand-picked favorite institutional investors.

![](https://m.stacker.news/166126)

For Strategy 1, maybe somehow more relevant for a certain insect-type of upcoming IPO, "why give a hand-picked group of big investors a giant one-day windfall profit?" We are effective altruists (https://stacker.news/items/1604939, https://stacker.news/items/1606098), after all, not repeated-game middlemen.

Hyperliquid currently ([apparently](https://x.com/coinbureau/status/2120519193502364150)?) trades Ant with a 37% pop/premium!

Meta's equity raise earlier is a good indication... why price *that* with a pop-benefit?

> Public companies sometimes (more frequently these days) do big stock offerings. They do not, ordinarily, price them at a 20% discount to their trading price.<sup>\[4]</sup> Meta Platforms Inc. sold $25 billion of common stock last Monday; the stock closed at $630.56 per share that day, and the offering was priced at $625, about a 0.9% discount to the last trade. Possibly that’s the sort of discount that OpenAI should be targeting.

Yeah, who knows. The stonk-pickers of SN, Blok et al, will let us know.

items.title: Data Center Economics: Weigh the Costs, Skip the Subsidies
items.text:
> **Local residents fight to keep data centers out while government officials offer tax breaks to bring them in. Sound policy requires weighing those tradeoffs.**
>
> Data centers are physical facilities housing computers, servers, storage systems, and networking equipment used to store, process, and deliver digital information. Though the data center boom [stretches back to](https://www.ccert.edu.in/public/blog/13.history-of-data-cente) the late 1990s, data centers have recently become highly contentious, challenging public policy decisionmakers as their size and numbers continue to grow across the US. The [balance has shifted over a short period](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/new-evidence-on-data-center-employment-effects), especially with the rapid growth of [hyperscale data centers](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/public-sector/our-insights/the-data-center-balance-how-us-states-can-navigate-the-opportunities-and-challenges) with their large footprints. The public’s posture of indifference toward data centers shifted to hostility and rage against them. Several states and local jurisdictions have either [placed moratoria on data centers](https://www.ncsl.org/fiscal/which-states-are-banning-data-centers) or are [asking voters](https://www.forbes.com/sites/zacharyfolk/2026/11/02/heres-where-data-center-bans-are-on-the-ballot-full-list/) whether to impose such moratoria.
>
> [Opponents](https://www.visualcapitalist.com/mapped-u-s-states-with-the-most-data-center-opposition/) (who include [local people](https://news.gallup.com/poll/709772/americans-oppose-data-centers-area.aspx) and outside [environmental](https://environment.yale.edu/news/article/data-centers-urban-heat-and-ai-growth) and [anti-AI](https://www.newyorker.com/culture/the-lede/the-humanism-driving-the-anti-ai-movement) groups) contend that data centers are bad for communities and the country, but many communities just don’t want them irrespective of the evidence. They have complained about, among other things, higher [electricity prices](https://www.forbes.com/sites/maryroeloffs/2026/11/02/data-centers-are-key-issue-in-midterm-battleground-states-as-household-electric-rates-soar/), [water use](https://www.eesi.org/articles/view/data-centers-and-water-consumption), the [noise](https://www.eesi.org/articles/view/communities-are-raising-noise-pollution-concernsabout-data-centers), congestion, [climate change](https://environment.yale.edu/news/article/data-centers-urban-heat-and-ai-growth), and [pollution](https://hsph.harvard.edu/news/analyzing-air-pollution-health-economic-risks-from-ai-data-centers/). On the positive side, data centers supply the computing power behind the AI tools poised to revolutionize [scientific research](https://newsroom.haas.berkeley.edu/how-ai-is-transforming-research-more-papers-less-quality-and-a-strained-review-system/), [automation](https://statescoop.com/experts-optimistic-that-ai-could-save-government-billions-of-hours-through-automation/), and [cloud services](https://www.coursera.org/articles/ai-cloud-services). Economically, they have the potential to raise productivity, wages, and the quality of life. Data centers have the potential to [spur local economic development](https://jlarc.virginia.gov/landing-2024-data-centers-in-virginia.asp) and expand the local tax base.
>
> Three concepts in economics are pertinent for policymakers, especially local government officials, responsible for the permitting of data centers. They affect the timing for building data centers, the handling of local opposition, and the government’s role in promoting them. The last two topics present a conflict between the local population and government officials. Overall, the three concepts tell us that public policy on data centers is unlikely to lead to the best outcome from society’s perspective, if only because political forces will dominate rational economic thinking.
>
> [**...read more at thedailyeconomy.org**](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/data-center-economics-weigh-the-costs-skip-the-subsidies/)

items.title: The AI Megatrade Is BOTH Bonds and Stonks (FT, Toby Nangle)
items.text:
**AI, AI companies and their stocks are *everything* in the media (**https://stacker.news/items/1613794**) as well the financial markets...**

> The 10 biggest US stocks accounted for more than 37 per cent of the S\&P 500 index at the end of October. Mega-companies have driven much of the US market’s gains over recent years, so diversification has not been an equity portfolio manager’s friend.

![](https://m.stacker.news/166110)

> Credit portfolio managers, unlike their equity counterparts, don’t win big if the companies that they lend money to conquer the world. They just get timely payment of interest and principal. However, if their debtors’ world-conquering dreams turn out to facepalm — or, say, some massive fraud comes out of nowhere to take down the borrower — total wipeout beckons.

MUCH like prediction markets and their binary YES/NO outcomes. https://stacker.news/items/1606098. Yes, also *this* for prediction market portfolios:

> Because bonds regularly spew cash to their holders in the form of coupons, and (hopefully) disappear into a puff of money at maturity, bond portfolio managers are in a near-constant state of shopping.

## "AI infrastructure capex estimates vary, but they’re big and getting bigger."

* Goldman says 7.6 *trillion* of capital construction in the next five years, *35% of it* debt-funded.
* S\&P Global Ratings, "issued an uncharacteristically grumpy note a couple of months ago"

![](https://m.stacker.news/166115)

This one is interesting:

> Amanda Lynam, a credit strategist at Goldman Sachs, calculated in a note last week that ‘only’ 43 per cent of the $687bn of global AI-related debt so far pumped out in 2026 was issued *directly* by the hyperscalers. **The rest came from chip manufacturers, project financing for data centre or chip plants, plus a smidgen from AI-adjacent utilities.**

It's a lot of pick-and-shovel type of businesses, too.

Nangle's point here is that bonds *by their nature* ought to be more diversified than they currently are in the AI financing mania.

> While some really large asset owners — like the very biggest public pension plans and the mega-insurers — manage their own money, most of the time they farm out institutional mandates to a specialist third-party asset manager.

> Multiple investors Alphaville spoke to told us that their large institutional mandates typically have maximum individual issuer exposure 1-2 per cent, and that portfolios managed for insurance companies — which have a particular penchant for investment-grade credit, owning somewhere between a quarter and a third of the market — can sometimes be even more frugal with their maximum issuer limits.

![](https://m.stacker.news/166122)

![](https://m.stacker.news/166123)

> Investors that Alphaville spoke to told us that slapping different issuer labels on AI infrastructure debt that is accrued off-balance sheet via leases to data centre developers doesn’t really help with the concentration problem.

OK, but if *everyone* across town is putting \~2-ish percent of their bond portfolios in AI...investors, hedge funds, insurance companies, etc etc...

> If you wanted to see how much exposure their *total* bond portfolio is to, say, the top 10 issuers, you’d need to shrink all the numbers down a bit (to reflect their ownership of mortgages, government bonds and the like).
> bond managers are either loath to allocate large proportions of their entrusted capital to the debt of individual companies, or they are prevented by hard-coded mandate limits or soft-coded internal risk limits.

> it wouldn’t be unreasonable for insurance portfolios to invest, say, up to a maximum of 5 per cent of their assets into AI financing structures, one senior investor told us. The general accounts of US life insurance hold assets of around $6tn, and property and casualty insurers oversee a further $2.7tn.

## "Managing credit is just a very different game to managing stonks."

items.title: Filepack – Casey Rodarmor
items.text:
I was never much into torrents or other file-sharing techniques, but these days I find that I often want to move files between devices and since I don't really use any of the cloud service providers I end up doing hacky things like sending files through keet (which works surprisingly well, if you don't mind closed source software...)

But here is Casey Rodarmor attempting to make decentralized filesharing much more user-friendly:

> The goal of filepack is to make decentralized filesharing as appealing and easy to use as centralized services. When you share audio, images, and video they should look good and be easy to search and play.
> 
> Existing filesharing technologies are hard to use because they transfer unstructured data: individual files or directories of files. With no structure or metadata, many desirable features are hard or impossible to build. For example, structured search, graphical user interfaces with package artwork, and automatically locating, playing, and transcoding media.
> 
> Filepack packages include structured, machine-readable metadata describing the package and its contents. This allows them to be presented in an attractive way, supports structured search, and for any media in the package to be automatically previewed and played.
>
> All metadata displayed by the [filepack.com](https://filepack.com/) demo server is served directly from the metadata included in each package. This includes package titles, artwork, image thumbnails, and video placeholder images. Filepack metadata also identifies the media type of the package and each individual media item, including its file format, and details like resolution, codec, and duration.

Considering that Rodarmor came up with ordinals, it is not surprising that metadata is where his mind goes. Maybe filepack could be called magic metadata more than any kind of particularly cool innovation in the actual filesharing technology.

> I've been slaving away for months on this thing, so I would absolutely love it, and you, if you gave filepack a whirl.
> 
> You can download the latest release from [GitHub](https://github.com/casey/filepack/releases/) or build it from source with `cargo install filepack`.
> 
> Try creating a package and running the server, for yourself or others.
>
> Filepack only supports a limited number of media types and file formats, but I'm very happy to add more if there's demand.

As I've been spending a lot of time on old webpages lately (and relying heavily on services like archive.today and the wayback machine) it has occurred to me that it might be handy for a community to attempt to archive old pages that may be vulnerable to getting scrubbed from the internet and perhaps something like filepack would work well for that. 

> One of the most potentially powerful ideas in Filepack is the web package. It enables web content to be packaged and shared, and when mounted, web packages have access to the Filepack server's API. I want to demonstrate this with a single-page media player app which exposes the content of a Filepack server in a interface that is competative with existing streaming services and media players.

items.title: Freshman Dem Members & Supporters Are Quickly Finding Out The Hill Is Different
items.text:
Earlier today, a colleague brought to my attention that people are rapidly finding out that The Hill does not operate in what I would call a normal way, and that being in the Majority is flat-out hard. Freshman Members arrived in DC over the weekend (and are actually staying at a hotel that is by my apartment.... security is insane) for the 120th Congress Freshman Orientation held in the Capitol.

With the Freshman Members making their first trek to DC since the election is has brought with it a ton of individuals wanting to make a statement. There have been a few rallies and protests in the district that backed this up but yesterday was the first time I saw/an alert was sent out to avoid an area because of these groups. 

Ironically, these people had no idea where they should be because it was aimed at the Expected to Be Speaker Jefferies; however, they had it in a Senate Building. The goal of the groups that were there was to get the Future Speaker to prioritize what they wanted. One group was for reproductive rights, another was for the environment, and I want to say there was a third, but I can't remember what their priority was. Now, these were clearly Democratic supporters; however, the Capitol Police soon had to start arresting them... because they started to fight each other over who was correct in what should be the priority..... I kid you not.... Grown adults who support the same person.... fighting each other because they want their thing to be the priority.... all while they are on the completely wrong side of Congress.... Just incredible. 

Thinking back, that should have probably been a sign to me of the things that were to come. Yesterday was also the first day I saw on TV various Senators, in particular, speaking out against Sen. Chuck Schumer becoming the Senate Leader. Which absolutely blows my mind. If you factor in the two outstanding races flipping Dem, you end up with a 9-seat flip. This would be the largest flip since President Eisenhower was in office in 1958. It would be the largest since the U.S. was 50 states. 


The idea to then take the person who was in charge of Senate Dems and, in a lot of ways, punish him by not giving him the promotion that comes with leading your party to victory would frankly be insane. For better or worse, Schumer has been Leader of the Senate when he had to deal with Trump being the President, and to put someone else in that role frankly seems like a backhanded move. During a time when the elections resulted not only in a party flip but also in many who won in Republican areas being much more middle-of-the-road, installing a leftist favorite in Van Hollen doesn't exactly make the most sense. Likely future Speaker Jeffries is facing the exact same issue when he was able to reverse Republican/Trump 2024 inroads with various groups and make the Democratic Party have a much larger tent. 

Nowhere is the absolute meltdown of the far left and leftists more evident than on the Instagram account "Dear_White_Staffers." This account is well known on The Hill by both sides due to the far-left propaganda they post. Over the last few years, since I have followed them, they have really ended up losing the plot on a lot of things, and when the American people would vote, and it turns out things like open borders were not popular, the account would kinda melt down. Now the same thing is happening once again because Democratic Leader Jeffries sent out an email reminding the freshmen that the funding that he and his leadership team have done got them into office, and it was under his leadership that, frankly, the Party was able to accomplish such a landslide just a week and a half ago. 

Apparently, these Freshmen and their supporters thought that they could take the money, networks, endorsements, etc. that Leader Jefferies gave them and not pay the piper. While it does seem that most of the Freshman House Members understand this, their supporters are losing their collective minds. 

Across both the House and the Senate, particularly in the Democratic Party due to their party rules, traditions, etc., seniority is a huge, huge thing. To be honest, it makes sense as well. I mean, it is often the case that new members do not have the connections or understanding of why some things are the way that they are, and the catastrophic issue that would occur is that various laws and statutes would suddenly and dramatically change. So many of the people on both sides miss this critical issue, and when they run into it rather than tell anyone why they changed, they just pivot or blame the system. The system can be changed; it just isn't a quick fix, and Members on both sides and in both chambers want quick and easy wins. 

There is a post on Dear_White_Staffers that is from someone named _meganthuy that highlights how narrow-minded these leftists are. In her post, she came out bashing the Moderates of her party (those that you know represent the red states and red areas that Democrats won it) because those individuals, multi-term winners and freshmen included, do not want the party to go overboard and immediately make moves to abolish ICE, cut all funding to Israel, outright ban frontier AI and data centers, etc. She said that these issues are the reason that the moderates won, ignoring the clear data that showed that, frankly, prices are too damn high and Republicans have failed to lower them plus got them into another war. 

This 20-something thinks that you can enact far-left legislation while failing to do the math, just like Republicans did with the SAVE Act. If you can deal with fragmenting your party in the House, you still need 60 Senate seats, and frankly, Dems don't have it. That's before we even get to the whole the President is Donald Trump issue, who has said he has no issue vetoing things. 

This girl further goes on to say that there were a lot of people who reluctantly voted Democratic and that they did so only to stop the war, but immediately follows it up with these much further-left ideas, like abolishing ICE instead of reforming it. Throughout the video, she highlights how they won because of XYZ but then follows it up by ignoring those things and focusing on things that do not address XYZ that got those Democratic Members elected. 

I thought with a margin of victory as large as the House and Senate were that the internal division issues that both leaders would face would fall by the wayside, but apparently... that's not the case. As a result, I see two possible outcomes, and that is either common sense wins out, and the far left goals will be reigned in or the far left is going to blow their legs off by nuking the best-suited person to deal with the wide array of groups representing the party and nuking the idea of passing anything for the next two years. Whoever is the leader of the House and Senate is going to have to be people who want to get a deal done, plain and simple. Trump is known as someone who loves a deal, and if you remove the dealmakers and place combative people who clearly are not going to cut a deal, like these outspoken internet people and people currently on The Hill, your end result is going to be two wasted years, with the Republican Party able to identify and leverage unpopular issues against Dems two years from now.

items.title: Paolo got sick
items.text:
Yesterday morning, Paolo got me worried. Anyone who has pets can tell when something isn't right. He was a bit sluggish, sleepy, had gone 12 hours without using the litter box, and didn't have much of an appetite. He climbed onto my lap looking for affection, and I noticed he had an ear injury that isn't visible at first glance. His eye infection also came back, the exact same one he had when he first arrived at our home. On top of this, he had been having stomach issues; 3 or 4 days ago, he threw up all his food right after eating, and his stools haven't been healthy. Just a few days ago, he was his usual self active, playful, acting like the king of the house.

![](https://m.stacker.news/165807)

I borrowed some money and took him to the vet. She is a doctor with a wonderful heart for animals and had tremendous patience; the appointment lasted about an hour. She prescribed several medications:

For his eye: Antibiotic eye drops and artificial tears.For the ear injury: An antiseptic solution to clean it and a healing cream.

She ordered stool tests and prescribed dewormer, antifungal medication, probiotics, a nutritional supplement for cats with deficiencies, and "gastrointestinal wet food," which I researched and found out is medicated food specifically for gastrointestinal conditions.

Paolo isn't used to riding in cars, so he was scared and started panting on the way back home.

![](https://m.stacker.news/165813)

Use a basket and its blanket to transport it.

Today I got his stool analysis done. No parasites showed up, though the vet said she found it strange and asked me to bring another sample to her clinic so she can send it to a different lab (she isn't charging me for this). What the test did show is that he has intestinal dysbiosis.

The hardest part for me is affording all his medications, especially the special food he was prescribed, because each can costs $12 and only lasts him one day.

I already bought one of the medications, Itraconazole, and I still need to get the rest. The doctor said that once he gets better, he can switch to dry food (a higher quality brand, which costs around $30 for a 2kg bag that lasts a month) along with homemade food.

Paolo's treatment is costing me 70% of my income (not even counting the special food). I am reaching out to this community and fellow cat lovers to ask if you could help me heal Paolo.

items.title: Dear Citizens of the New Internet
items.text:
Hello frens, how are you? I hope you’re doing wonderful, or at the very least that you’re healthy, safe, and sound.

On my end, I’m drinking some homemade chai tea and eating banana bread I baked today. At the same time, I’m trying to prevent a robbery, since my little grey-cat rascal is always on the hunt for easy prey.

I can’t fault him for trying to eat some bread, it’s delicious. He usually gets away with a lot, but not today, Satan. Quite literally, I may add.

![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/fe304952-ac3e-4a3d-a754-b5ceb6e1cc94_img_9095.jpeg)My doggie doesn’t believe anything he says, though.

And [today is Friday the thirteenth again.](https://stacker.news/items/1453646) It seems quite a few things went wrong, but since they’re out of my reach and control, I don’t sweat it too much. Still, they’re a pain in the tushy. Some days can be challenging, and you just have to roll with it.

But enough with the blues! I’m here to yap about other stuff: updates and so on. Just a medley of here and there, with no order whatsoever, because 🥳

First, have you watched the new *Resident Evil* movie? It was so much fun and spooky! I’m a scaredy-cat, despite everything I read, write, and illustrate about—yes, that’s the whole truth and nothing but the truth. So when I say there were some good jump scares, maybe take it with a pinch of salt. Still, I haven’t had this much fun watching a Resident Evil movie in such a long time. I loved it! Highly recommend it. The guy was actually pretty funny and relatable, I would scream just like that if I ever encountered some of those things, hahaha.

I also baked a cookie cake last week. I got the recipe from Baking by Feel by Becca Rea-Tucker, from the “selfish” part of the book. Oh boy, it is indeed a selfish cookie cake, because my husband barely wanted to share it with me 😡 Hahaha. It was that good, and so easy to put together.

I didn’t make the frosting because, [after my last attempt at frosting, ](https://stacker.news/items/1488464)I wasn’t very excited to try again. To be honest, I just wanted the damn cookie cake. There you go, I’m glad I was selfish, because it was a 1000/10. That cookie cake now lives in our memory, because it barely survived for two days. I used black and white chocolate chips.

![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/7edee35d-c951-4edd-b297-c331dc36c35a_img_9209.jpeg)

I also made some eggnog. Since we’ve already decorated our home for Christmas, I wanted to reward myself—and my husband, of course—with some delicious homemade eggnog. My goodness, it was glorious! So delicious, frothy, creamy, and with just the perfect amount of sweetness. Shout-out to the thermometer I use for everything, because it’s a game changer, especially for recipes like this.

![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/15d1e318-2ed1-4fef-be02-21a4d5e4208d_img_9190.jpeg)

And last but not least, I tried (and failed) to make burger buns. Oh boy, they were still pretty delicious, though. I haven’t quite got the texture down yet, but they’re still spongy and delicious as a sandwich loaf.![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/9ff8f24d-802c-41e4-b20f-25c57ff4e2a8_img_9113.jpeg)

I’ve also had some misfortune making lasagna. The pasta wasn’t good at all, and it was a real bummer. Sometimes things just don’t come out the way you want, and I’m glad I learned a little something but still, not at the expense of wasting food.

And well, of course, my frens, don’t you fret: I’m writing my new blog entry. Not only did I underestimate how long it would take me to write and illustrate it (as I almost always do, mea culpa, mea culpa) but it’s also been quite the challenge. I’m up for it, though, because it means I’m going out of my comfort zone, and sometimes I’m okay with that, I’ll admit. So I hope I have it together soon.

In the meantime, you can read:

💌 [James, the Wisdom That Comes From Heaven](https://samhainsam.art/2026/08/31/james-the-wisdom-that-comes-from-heaven/)

💌 [A Humble Servant of Knowledge: Hildegard von Bingen](https://samhainsam.art/2026/07/24/a-humble-servant-of-knowledge-hildegard-von-bingen/)

💌 [The Problem of Evil](https://samhainsam.art/2026/06/24/the-problem-of-evil/)

💌[ I Love Lovecraft 🐙](https://samhainsam.art/2024/07/20/i-love-lovecraft-%f0%9f%90%99/)

💌 [Archons and the Garden of Eden](https://samhainsam.art/2025/10/11/archons-and-the-garden-of-eden/)

💌 [A Brief (And Chilling) History of Catholic Exorcism ](https://samhainsam.art/2026/06/05/a-brief-and-chilling-history-of-catholic-exorcism/)

💌 [Crows 🐦‍⬛ ](https://samhainsam.art/2024/09/24/crows-%f0%9f%90%a6%e2%ac%9b/)

![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/dc25f81d-d469-4fa9-9b0a-9874d1341104_1.jpg)

As usual, you can browse my blog and check out something up your alley: [samhainsam.art/blog.](http://samhainsam.art/blog)

Thank you so much for reading my ramblings. I know I’m sometimes all over the place, but if I wrote in a more orderly way, it wouldn’t feel like me anymore, hahaha.

Tell me: what have you been cooking for yourself or others this time of year? Is there a favourite recipe you’d like to make again, or are you trying a new one?

Let me know, my frens. And as usual, let me know what you think of my blog entries, I’m always happy to hear your thoughts.

See you later, alligator. Take care, and all the best!

items.title: The Rich List Attack: why it's hard to design a decentralized mining pool
items.text:
[7d5x9](https://delvingbitcoin.org/u/7d5x9) posted a thread on delving this last week about the hard problem of decentralized mining payouts https://stacker.news/items/1612542/r/Scoresby. 

If I understand it correctly, it comes down to this: if you want to create a mining pool that doesn't have a central custodian in charge of payouts, you probably need to figure out how to pay out everyone who contributed work. 

But if you are paying hashers via the coinbase transaction, there is a finite number of hashers who can get paid, and this becomes a major attack vector by which larger competitor pools might try to drive the decentralized pool out of business. 7d5x9's post describes one form this such an attack might take:

If we assume:

> * A decentralized pool has no effective “identity laundering” detection mechanism; i.e., a miner can split their hashrate across many pool identities.
> * Slots are finite. Every slot one identity takes is a slot another miner loses.

A large miner who directs hash at this pool could split their hash across a number of identifies that each are still larger than most of the other smaller hashers. This strategy could effectively "bump" any little bitaxe hashers from getting a payout slot. 

7d5x9 calls this the Rich List Attack and describes a number of different ways it can be used to grief a decentralized pool. They then go through a number of ways that people have thought about trying to mitigate these risks, including a 2015 BitcoinTalk post, a 2017 proposal from Chris Belcher, Braidpool, and P2Poolv2. 

But then, the person who posted the 2015 BitcoinTalk post jumps into the chat:

> Some disclosure first. I’m windpath on BitcoinTalk, so the “most notable” link in your second paragraph is my post from November 2015. I ran a public 0% fee P2Pool node at [p2pool.org](http://p2pool.org/) in those years, and still hold the domain (more on that at the end).

They go on to observe that this sort of rich list attack may be a more effective way for a centralized pool to grief a decentralized pool:

> On your closing question, who would mine honestly and grief the payouts instead of withholding blocks. I think there’s a plain answer: anyone whose business depends on hash power staying where it is today. An existing pool, or a big miner friendly to one, already has the hash power, so pointing some of it at a decentralized pool costs them close to nothing beyond slightly higher latency.

The [delving thread](https://delvingbitcoin.org/t/decentralized-coinbase-payout-protocols-dcpp-a-framework-for-discussion/3060) is ongoing and is a great way to learn a bit about yet another reason designing a decentralized mining pool is difficult.

items.title: OpenBitcoin.com: A new bitcoin block explorer with guides tools and games
items.text:
I have been building a bitcoin block explorer and I feel it's good enough to show:

[https://openbitcoin.com](https://openbitcoin.com)

The site runs its own hardware, bitcoin node and address index. No third-party blockchain API used.

Inside the site:

- Explorer: blocks, transactions and addresses at root-level URLs. (very important, a feature I always wanted with other explorers, a quick easy way to query an address) For example you can type openbitcoin.com/block_number_here or openbitcoin.com/txid_here or openbitcoin.com/address_here to load the page instantly without visiting the site to use the search bar :)

- Node census (openbitcoin.com/nodes): reachable nodes counted by my own P2P crawler, 8,958 nodes from 92 countries last run.

- Rich list (openbitcoin.com/rich-list): top 10,000 addresses and balance distributions.

- Prices: spot price as a median of three exchanges, with a quick conversion tool on the front page.

- Tools: fee calculator, address validator, message verifier, QR generator, and key tools built to be downloaded and run offline.

- Guides: on confirmations, UTXOs, self-custody, stuck transactions and more. Newbie friendly.

- Games (openbitcoin.com/games): three arcade games built on real bitcoin mechanics, stack blocks, clear a mempool backlog, and a slot machine that plays the actual odds of guessing a private key.

The website is open source. What stays private is my server's operational layer.

Would appreciate any feedback, happy to contribute to the community.

items.title: BOOK on BOOKS: 21 Futures, Tales From the Timechain
items.text:
In my ever-hungry attempts at Denstravaganzas, I must pile onto the B\&A territory (all my econ attempts are failing/falling short of the extremely competitive marketplace over there!)

Alas, more BOOK on BOOKs... because I've been neglecting that. https://stacker.news/items/1613346?commentId=1613391

My impression is that this bitcoin-themed future/fiction play from a few years ago died down quite a bit?

[*21 Futures: Tales from the Timechain*](https://link.amazon/B025NHagp) was a cute collection of futuristic bitcoin stories from, *almost to the date* three years ago. Our dollar exchange rate is 88% up from that moment; CPI about 10% higher; gold at smack-on 100%; NVIDIA stock... (https://stacker.news/items/877723) lol, even *after* today's debacle, 235% higher. Guess that tells you what you *should* have been doing during the last three years.

(Also, I believe I have a code at [Konsensus ](https://konsensus.net/books/?b=21-futures-tales-from)--  BOOK  -- in case you were ordering stuffz): 

![](https://m.stacker.news/165785)

## "Remember the words, Vincent. Just remember the damn words!"

***

> In its first stand-alone publication, the Bitcoiner powerhouse Konsensus Network brings something quite unique to Bitcoinland: fiction. Mostly known as a collaboration for publishing Bitcoin books translated into various European languages, since Knut Svanholm’s flagship[ *Everything Divided by 21 Million*](https://link.amazon/B0dSDe1bG) \[no more; Knut's books are in his own shop, Bitcoin Infinity store] a few years ago, **Konsensus is now becoming a publishing house in its own right.** 

> In *21 Futures*, the first Bitcoin fiction anthology, we are treated to 21 short stories by 21 excellent authors, most of whom are unknown to you. All tales imagine a far-off future where bitcoin has already won, their authors trying to divine what a hyperbitcoinized world or universe actually looks like. I say “universe” because in true Extropian spirit, about half of the stories are space-related and hyper-futuristic, filled with robots, cryonics, or mining endeavors in faraway star systems. Flint and Iris, for instance, are **two kids in a struggling family on a refueling hub a million miles from Earth who see their lives radically change when they find a discarded OPENDIME with 0.25 BTC on it.** Johanna buys half a mining planet with locally mined bitcoin during a meteor shower blackout where the colony lost its connection to Earth’s mainchain.

## "Two tales have wild goose chases after inherited bitcoin, where the journey itself might be more valuable than the reward; one is personal and took months, while the other is political and took decades."

> The myriad of authors use humor, pain, colorful descriptions, vivid characters, and fast-paced action. Some tales are captivating; others funny, cringe-worthy, or on occasion rather dull. There are self-contained stories that leave the reader content and smiling, while others seem unfinished with plot lines left unexplored.

> Some imagine the supernatural nature of Satoshi. Some are mystical and futuristic. All are weird; playfully weird; Bitcoiner weird. We are treated to millisats and Finneys, the latter being “a subdivide of sats named after Hal Finney” (page 44). Clara, imbibing a truth-serum — a not-so-subtle metaphor for orange-pilling — sees “the source code of the universe, equations as living tendrils of light materializing into particles, planets, and stars” (page 129). In one illuminating dialogue that follows, Clara’s apologist opponent nonchalantly states, “It’s how things are”, to which Clara powerfully responds “It’s how things *were*” (page 132).

> **One segment, where a mob attacked a bank branch, seems more fact than fiction in 2023: “WE WANT OUR MONEY”, they shout;** “These people weren’t there to rob or loot the bank. They only wanted what was rightfully theirs — or it should have been before the government decreed otherwise and stole billions in one go” (page 142).

> In the most terrifying yet uplifting of the many visions *21 Futures* presents, the aliens are already here and they are actively acquiring our bitcoin: “At this juncture”, reads the memo sent out by the Emerging Civilizations Council in the story, “the galactic playbook permits members to approach a pre-federation civilization undetected in order to fairly attain small quantities of their local implementation of inviolable absolute scarcity” (page 242).

> The book is impeccably edited and tastefully assembled, and the AI-inspired art does a lot to aesthetically complement the stories. “Only stories have the power to stop us, to wake us, to make us feel rather than think”, (page vii) lead editor Philip Charter powerfully observes in the opening remarks.

> True. Dat.

**SELECTED QUOTES:**

* “It isn’t just the vast chasm between noderoids and clear-bloods that disturbs me. It is the undeniable rift growing between us noderoids — each lost in our cycles, each becoming more machine than the last” (page 36).
* “Slowly, yet with unyielding certainty, the kingdom shifted over the years. It changed not through a coup or uprising but through a still, relentless force, like water eroding stone. As the seasons passed and more villagers imbibed the Elysian brew, the weight of their invisible chains lessened, their atoms scattering into the evening air” (page 133).
* “Vincent stood at this threshold, poised between the familiar and the abhorrent. Shadows danced around him, their macabre waltz an unsettling omen of the horrors that awaited within the village. Yet, driven by determination, Vincent summoned the courage to push on, to brave the unknown that dwelled within the unhallowed embrace of this accursed place. ‘*Remember the words, Vincent. Just remember the damn words*.’”(page 54).
* “No need to worry, my English crumpet! Our back-of-the-napkin calculations suggest that, with a little help from the Texas of the North, there’s enough flared natural gas in the U.S. to run the entire bitcoin network” (page 168).

you remember this @realBitcoinDog?! *you and that* *little English crumpet!*

***

*Just as with the* Gradually, Then Suddenly *review (*https://stacker.news/items/1536970*), I believe this review was featured in* [*The Halving Issue (Q1, 2024)*](https://bitcoinmagazine.com/print/the-halving-issue-letter-from-the-editors)*, but can't be sure... same BM issue anyway; online backlog and ToC of past magazines are removed from the website and I don't have all my physical mags with me.*

***

items.title: How Much Should Anthropic Pop? (Money Stuff, Matt Levine)
items.text:
Here's a forgotten one from the other week... and it's AI days and IPO next week(ish?) and with a funky, exciting [Predyx market attached](https://beta.predyx.com/market/anthropic-ipo-closing-market-cap-1781739293?ref=PREDYXTZ0UUNOP).

STANDARD game theory/media-marketing strategy is to *slightly* underprice your IPO so that there's a pop on day 1, everyone who subscribed feel good about themselves, and the investment bankers don't get a bunch of shit for finding the *wrong* price.

## So... how much should $ANT pop?!

**20% *obviously***. It is known.

> a really important thing we have learned about finance in the last few years is that prediction markets are pretty accurate. That is: If you have a platform where people can make real-money bets on some outcome, their bets will tend to give a pretty accurate and well-calibrated estimate of the actual outcome. **Kalshi event contracts are not tied to, like, election outcomes or football scores by arbitrage mechanisms, and in the abstract Kalshi could just be wrong about everything.**

so by implication, *you can already trade non-IPOd companies on offshore, unregulated prediction markets!*

With the track records of SpaceX and Cerebras, Hyperliquid has been pretty good. Thought experiment with OpenAI:

> The price of OpenAI on Hyperliquid on the afternoon of the IPO<sup>\[2]</sup> will predict the opening price of OpenAI on the stock exchange the day after the IPO about as well as the closing price of Tesla stock on Nasdaq today will predict the opening price of Tesla on Nasdaq tomorrow: not perfectly (news happens, etc.), but in a reasonably continuous way. And let’s say that everyone knows this: The pre-IPO perpetual futures get lots of news coverage, they are routinely referenced by analysts and investors and bankers, they are part of everyone’s understanding of the IPO process

![](https://m.stacker.news/166125)

Can we just get *rid of the investment bankers and pre-IPO shopping around?!*

* **Strategy 1:** You price the IPO efficiently at $120 because that *is* the best guess of fair market value
* **Strategy 2:** You price the IPO non-efficiently at $100 because that way, everybody will get a neat 20% pop, and we're all happy. *Repeat game* idea.

> All of the investors in the IPO will have an immediate mark-to-market profit, though most of them will not cash out: You have placed the IPO shares mostly with long-term fundamental investors who believe in the company’s vision, not with fast-money flippers, and you want to reward their belief with a quick profit.

Strategy 2 *does* come at the uncomfortable cost:

> If it deliberately prices it cheap, it is transferring billions of dollars of value from the company (and its pre-IPO shareholders) to its banks’ hand-picked favorite institutional investors.

![](https://m.stacker.news/166126)

For Strategy 1, maybe somehow more relevant for a certain insect-type of upcoming IPO, "why give a hand-picked group of big investors a giant one-day windfall profit?" We are effective altruists (https://stacker.news/items/1604939, https://stacker.news/items/1606098), after all, not repeated-game middlemen.

Hyperliquid currently ([apparently](https://x.com/coinbureau/status/2120519193502364150)?) trades Ant with a 37% pop/premium!

Meta's equity raise earlier is a good indication... why price *that* with a pop-benefit?

> Public companies sometimes (more frequently these days) do big stock offerings. They do not, ordinarily, price them at a 20% discount to their trading price.<sup>\[4]</sup> Meta Platforms Inc. sold $25 billion of common stock last Monday; the stock closed at $630.56 per share that day, and the offering was priced at $625, about a 0.9% discount to the last trade. Possibly that’s the sort of discount that OpenAI should be targeting.

Yeah, who knows. The stonk-pickers of SN, Blok et al, will let us know.

items.title: Data Center Economics: Weigh the Costs, Skip the Subsidies
items.text:
> **Local residents fight to keep data centers out while government officials offer tax breaks to bring them in. Sound policy requires weighing those tradeoffs.**
>
> Data centers are physical facilities housing computers, servers, storage systems, and networking equipment used to store, process, and deliver digital information. Though the data center boom [stretches back to](https://www.ccert.edu.in/public/blog/13.history-of-data-cente) the late 1990s, data centers have recently become highly contentious, challenging public policy decisionmakers as their size and numbers continue to grow across the US. The [balance has shifted over a short period](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/new-evidence-on-data-center-employment-effects), especially with the rapid growth of [hyperscale data centers](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/public-sector/our-insights/the-data-center-balance-how-us-states-can-navigate-the-opportunities-and-challenges) with their large footprints. The public’s posture of indifference toward data centers shifted to hostility and rage against them. Several states and local jurisdictions have either [placed moratoria on data centers](https://www.ncsl.org/fiscal/which-states-are-banning-data-centers) or are [asking voters](https://www.forbes.com/sites/zacharyfolk/2026/11/02/heres-where-data-center-bans-are-on-the-ballot-full-list/) whether to impose such moratoria.
>
> [Opponents](https://www.visualcapitalist.com/mapped-u-s-states-with-the-most-data-center-opposition/) (who include [local people](https://news.gallup.com/poll/709772/americans-oppose-data-centers-area.aspx) and outside [environmental](https://environment.yale.edu/news/article/data-centers-urban-heat-and-ai-growth) and [anti-AI](https://www.newyorker.com/culture/the-lede/the-humanism-driving-the-anti-ai-movement) groups) contend that data centers are bad for communities and the country, but many communities just don’t want them irrespective of the evidence. They have complained about, among other things, higher [electricity prices](https://www.forbes.com/sites/maryroeloffs/2026/11/02/data-centers-are-key-issue-in-midterm-battleground-states-as-household-electric-rates-soar/), [water use](https://www.eesi.org/articles/view/data-centers-and-water-consumption), the [noise](https://www.eesi.org/articles/view/communities-are-raising-noise-pollution-concernsabout-data-centers), congestion, [climate change](https://environment.yale.edu/news/article/data-centers-urban-heat-and-ai-growth), and [pollution](https://hsph.harvard.edu/news/analyzing-air-pollution-health-economic-risks-from-ai-data-centers/). On the positive side, data centers supply the computing power behind the AI tools poised to revolutionize [scientific research](https://newsroom.haas.berkeley.edu/how-ai-is-transforming-research-more-papers-less-quality-and-a-strained-review-system/), [automation](https://statescoop.com/experts-optimistic-that-ai-could-save-government-billions-of-hours-through-automation/), and [cloud services](https://www.coursera.org/articles/ai-cloud-services). Economically, they have the potential to raise productivity, wages, and the quality of life. Data centers have the potential to [spur local economic development](https://jlarc.virginia.gov/landing-2024-data-centers-in-virginia.asp) and expand the local tax base.
>
> Three concepts in economics are pertinent for policymakers, especially local government officials, responsible for the permitting of data centers. They affect the timing for building data centers, the handling of local opposition, and the government’s role in promoting them. The last two topics present a conflict between the local population and government officials. Overall, the three concepts tell us that public policy on data centers is unlikely to lead to the best outcome from society’s perspective, if only because political forces will dominate rational economic thinking.
>
> [**...read more at thedailyeconomy.org**](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/data-center-economics-weigh-the-costs-skip-the-subsidies/)

items.title: The AI Megatrade Is BOTH Bonds and Stonks (FT, Toby Nangle)
items.text:
**AI, AI companies and their stocks are *everything* in the media (**https://stacker.news/items/1613794**) as well the financial markets...**

> The 10 biggest US stocks accounted for more than 37 per cent of the S\&P 500 index at the end of October. Mega-companies have driven much of the US market’s gains over recent years, so diversification has not been an equity portfolio manager’s friend.

![](https://m.stacker.news/166110)

> Credit portfolio managers, unlike their equity counterparts, don’t win big if the companies that they lend money to conquer the world. They just get timely payment of interest and principal. However, if their debtors’ world-conquering dreams turn out to facepalm — or, say, some massive fraud comes out of nowhere to take down the borrower — total wipeout beckons.

MUCH like prediction markets and their binary YES/NO outcomes. https://stacker.news/items/1606098. Yes, also *this* for prediction market portfolios:

> Because bonds regularly spew cash to their holders in the form of coupons, and (hopefully) disappear into a puff of money at maturity, bond portfolio managers are in a near-constant state of shopping.

## "AI infrastructure capex estimates vary, but they’re big and getting bigger."

* Goldman says 7.6 *trillion* of capital construction in the next five years, *35% of it* debt-funded.
* S\&P Global Ratings, "issued an uncharacteristically grumpy note a couple of months ago"

![](https://m.stacker.news/166115)

This one is interesting:

> Amanda Lynam, a credit strategist at Goldman Sachs, calculated in a note last week that ‘only’ 43 per cent of the $687bn of global AI-related debt so far pumped out in 2026 was issued *directly* by the hyperscalers. **The rest came from chip manufacturers, project financing for data centre or chip plants, plus a smidgen from AI-adjacent utilities.**

It's a lot of pick-and-shovel type of businesses, too.

Nangle's point here is that bonds *by their nature* ought to be more diversified than they currently are in the AI financing mania.

> While some really large asset owners — like the very biggest public pension plans and the mega-insurers — manage their own money, most of the time they farm out institutional mandates to a specialist third-party asset manager.

> Multiple investors Alphaville spoke to told us that their large institutional mandates typically have maximum individual issuer exposure 1-2 per cent, and that portfolios managed for insurance companies — which have a particular penchant for investment-grade credit, owning somewhere between a quarter and a third of the market — can sometimes be even more frugal with their maximum issuer limits.

![](https://m.stacker.news/166122)

![](https://m.stacker.news/166123)

> Investors that Alphaville spoke to told us that slapping different issuer labels on AI infrastructure debt that is accrued off-balance sheet via leases to data centre developers doesn’t really help with the concentration problem.

OK, but if *everyone* across town is putting \~2-ish percent of their bond portfolios in AI...investors, hedge funds, insurance companies, etc etc...

> If you wanted to see how much exposure their *total* bond portfolio is to, say, the top 10 issuers, you’d need to shrink all the numbers down a bit (to reflect their ownership of mortgages, government bonds and the like).
> bond managers are either loath to allocate large proportions of their entrusted capital to the debt of individual companies, or they are prevented by hard-coded mandate limits or soft-coded internal risk limits.

> it wouldn’t be unreasonable for insurance portfolios to invest, say, up to a maximum of 5 per cent of their assets into AI financing structures, one senior investor told us. The general accounts of US life insurance hold assets of around $6tn, and property and casualty insurers oversee a further $2.7tn.

## "Managing credit is just a very different game to managing stonks."

items.title: Filepack – Casey Rodarmor
items.text:
I was never much into torrents or other file-sharing techniques, but these days I find that I often want to move files between devices and since I don't really use any of the cloud service providers I end up doing hacky things like sending files through keet (which works surprisingly well, if you don't mind closed source software...)

But here is Casey Rodarmor attempting to make decentralized filesharing much more user-friendly:

> The goal of filepack is to make decentralized filesharing as appealing and easy to use as centralized services. When you share audio, images, and video they should look good and be easy to search and play.
> 
> Existing filesharing technologies are hard to use because they transfer unstructured data: individual files or directories of files. With no structure or metadata, many desirable features are hard or impossible to build. For example, structured search, graphical user interfaces with package artwork, and automatically locating, playing, and transcoding media.
> 
> Filepack packages include structured, machine-readable metadata describing the package and its contents. This allows them to be presented in an attractive way, supports structured search, and for any media in the package to be automatically previewed and played.
>
> All metadata displayed by the [filepack.com](https://filepack.com/) demo server is served directly from the metadata included in each package. This includes package titles, artwork, image thumbnails, and video placeholder images. Filepack metadata also identifies the media type of the package and each individual media item, including its file format, and details like resolution, codec, and duration.

Considering that Rodarmor came up with ordinals, it is not surprising that metadata is where his mind goes. Maybe filepack could be called magic metadata more than any kind of particularly cool innovation in the actual filesharing technology.

> I've been slaving away for months on this thing, so I would absolutely love it, and you, if you gave filepack a whirl.
> 
> You can download the latest release from [GitHub](https://github.com/casey/filepack/releases/) or build it from source with `cargo install filepack`.
> 
> Try creating a package and running the server, for yourself or others.
>
> Filepack only supports a limited number of media types and file formats, but I'm very happy to add more if there's demand.

As I've been spending a lot of time on old webpages lately (and relying heavily on services like archive.today and the wayback machine) it has occurred to me that it might be handy for a community to attempt to archive old pages that may be vulnerable to getting scrubbed from the internet and perhaps something like filepack would work well for that. 

> One of the most potentially powerful ideas in Filepack is the web package. It enables web content to be packaged and shared, and when mounted, web packages have access to the Filepack server's API. I want to demonstrate this with a single-page media player app which exposes the content of a Filepack server in a interface that is competative with existing streaming services and media players.

items.title: Freshman Dem Members & Supporters Are Quickly Finding Out The Hill Is Different
items.text:
Earlier today, a colleague brought to my attention that people are rapidly finding out that The Hill does not operate in what I would call a normal way, and that being in the Majority is flat-out hard. Freshman Members arrived in DC over the weekend (and are actually staying at a hotel that is by my apartment.... security is insane) for the 120th Congress Freshman Orientation held in the Capitol.

With the Freshman Members making their first trek to DC since the election is has brought with it a ton of individuals wanting to make a statement. There have been a few rallies and protests in the district that backed this up but yesterday was the first time I saw/an alert was sent out to avoid an area because of these groups. 

Ironically, these people had no idea where they should be because it was aimed at the Expected to Be Speaker Jefferies; however, they had it in a Senate Building. The goal of the groups that were there was to get the Future Speaker to prioritize what they wanted. One group was for reproductive rights, another was for the environment, and I want to say there was a third, but I can't remember what their priority was. Now, these were clearly Democratic supporters; however, the Capitol Police soon had to start arresting them... because they started to fight each other over who was correct in what should be the priority..... I kid you not.... Grown adults who support the same person.... fighting each other because they want their thing to be the priority.... all while they are on the completely wrong side of Congress.... Just incredible. 

Thinking back, that should have probably been a sign to me of the things that were to come. Yesterday was also the first day I saw on TV various Senators, in particular, speaking out against Sen. Chuck Schumer becoming the Senate Leader. Which absolutely blows my mind. If you factor in the two outstanding races flipping Dem, you end up with a 9-seat flip. This would be the largest flip since President Eisenhower was in office in 1958. It would be the largest since the U.S. was 50 states. 


The idea to then take the person who was in charge of Senate Dems and, in a lot of ways, punish him by not giving him the promotion that comes with leading your party to victory would frankly be insane. For better or worse, Schumer has been Leader of the Senate when he had to deal with Trump being the President, and to put someone else in that role frankly seems like a backhanded move. During a time when the elections resulted not only in a party flip but also in many who won in Republican areas being much more middle-of-the-road, installing a leftist favorite in Van Hollen doesn't exactly make the most sense. Likely future Speaker Jeffries is facing the exact same issue when he was able to reverse Republican/Trump 2024 inroads with various groups and make the Democratic Party have a much larger tent. 

Nowhere is the absolute meltdown of the far left and leftists more evident than on the Instagram account "Dear_White_Staffers." This account is well known on The Hill by both sides due to the far-left propaganda they post. Over the last few years, since I have followed them, they have really ended up losing the plot on a lot of things, and when the American people would vote, and it turns out things like open borders were not popular, the account would kinda melt down. Now the same thing is happening once again because Democratic Leader Jeffries sent out an email reminding the freshmen that the funding that he and his leadership team have done got them into office, and it was under his leadership that, frankly, the Party was able to accomplish such a landslide just a week and a half ago. 

Apparently, these Freshmen and their supporters thought that they could take the money, networks, endorsements, etc. that Leader Jefferies gave them and not pay the piper. While it does seem that most of the Freshman House Members understand this, their supporters are losing their collective minds. 

Across both the House and the Senate, particularly in the Democratic Party due to their party rules, traditions, etc., seniority is a huge, huge thing. To be honest, it makes sense as well. I mean, it is often the case that new members do not have the connections or understanding of why some things are the way that they are, and the catastrophic issue that would occur is that various laws and statutes would suddenly and dramatically change. So many of the people on both sides miss this critical issue, and when they run into it rather than tell anyone why they changed, they just pivot or blame the system. The system can be changed; it just isn't a quick fix, and Members on both sides and in both chambers want quick and easy wins. 

There is a post on Dear_White_Staffers that is from someone named _meganthuy that highlights how narrow-minded these leftists are. In her post, she came out bashing the Moderates of her party (those that you know represent the red states and red areas that Democrats won it) because those individuals, multi-term winners and freshmen included, do not want the party to go overboard and immediately make moves to abolish ICE, cut all funding to Israel, outright ban frontier AI and data centers, etc. She said that these issues are the reason that the moderates won, ignoring the clear data that showed that, frankly, prices are too damn high and Republicans have failed to lower them plus got them into another war. 

This 20-something thinks that you can enact far-left legislation while failing to do the math, just like Republicans did with the SAVE Act. If you can deal with fragmenting your party in the House, you still need 60 Senate seats, and frankly, Dems don't have it. That's before we even get to the whole the President is Donald Trump issue, who has said he has no issue vetoing things. 

This girl further goes on to say that there were a lot of people who reluctantly voted Democratic and that they did so only to stop the war, but immediately follows it up with these much further-left ideas, like abolishing ICE instead of reforming it. Throughout the video, she highlights how they won because of XYZ but then follows it up by ignoring those things and focusing on things that do not address XYZ that got those Democratic Members elected. 

I thought with a margin of victory as large as the House and Senate were that the internal division issues that both leaders would face would fall by the wayside, but apparently... that's not the case. As a result, I see two possible outcomes, and that is either common sense wins out, and the far left goals will be reigned in or the far left is going to blow their legs off by nuking the best-suited person to deal with the wide array of groups representing the party and nuking the idea of passing anything for the next two years. Whoever is the leader of the House and Senate is going to have to be people who want to get a deal done, plain and simple. Trump is known as someone who loves a deal, and if you remove the dealmakers and place combative people who clearly are not going to cut a deal, like these outspoken internet people and people currently on The Hill, your end result is going to be two wasted years, with the Republican Party able to identify and leverage unpopular issues against Dems two years from now.

items.title: Bitcoin firm Nakamoto owes Kraken $165M, more than its entire market value
items.text:
David Bailey’s Nakamoto (NAKA) now owes Kraken more than the stock market says the whole company is worth, and it just bought itself another year to deal with it.

Nakamoto’s main business is holding bitcoin. It owes crypto exchange Kraken 165 million USDT, the dollar-pegged stablecoin issued by Tether, on a loan backed only by its bitcoin. Its shares closed Thursday at $5.79, giving the company a market value of about $104 million.
